answer_text:
Let  
\[
f(x)=x^5+6x^3+8x+10.
\]

First determine \([\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]\). Compute the shifted polynomial:
\[
f(x+2)=x^5+10x^4+46x^3+116x^2+160x+106.
\]
All non-leading coefficients are divisible by \(2\), and \(2^2=4\) does not divide \(106\). Hence \(f(x+2)\) is Eisenstein at \(p=2\), so \(f(x+2)\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb{Q}\). Since the shift \(x\mapsto x+2\) preserves irreducibility, \(f(x)\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Thus \(\alpha\) has degree \(5\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\):
\[
[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=5.
\]

Since \(5\) is prime, \(\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)\) has no quadratic subfield. Therefore \(\sqrt{7}\notin \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)\), and
\[
[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha,\sqrt{7}):\mathbb{Q}]
=
[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]\,[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{7}):\mathbb{Q}]
=
5\cdot 2=10.
\]

The extension is separable because it is over \(\mathbb{Q}\), so the number of \(\mathbb{Q}\)-embeddings into \(\mathbb{C}\) equals the degree, which is \(10\).

\[
\boxed{10}
\]
